abstract: Ferns are widely distributed across nearly all major biomes and are indicators of ecosystem health and functioning. Therefore, their diversity and distributions can be used to elucidate the ecological and evolutionary mechanisms associated with net diversification and deep biogeographical events. Though Africa has relatively low fern species richness, the spatial patterns of fern diversity and distribution is non-random and may be indicative of the evolutionary history and paleo-ecological conditions that shape current floristic diversity on the continent. This study assessed spatial patterns of taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity of ferns in Africa. Using species occurrence records from biodiversity databases (Global Biodiversity Information Facility, the African Plants Portal, RAINBIO, and recently digitized specimens across 31 U.S. herbaria) and the Fern Tree of Life, we calculated and mapped several biodiversity measures including species richness, phylogenetic diversity (PD) and endemism (PE), relative phylogenetic diversity (RPD) and endemism (RPE), Sorensen-based phylogenetic and taxonomic beta diversity, and grade-of-membership models using phylogenetic and taxonomic distances. We also decomposed PE and RPE significance into different endemism centers using the categorical analysis of neo- and paleo-endemism (CANAPE) and investigated lineages driving patterns of endemism with the Range-weighted branch length difference metric (RWiBaLD). Finally, we investigate the association of contemporary climatic and soil factors and topography on spatial phylodiversity patterns of African ferns.
